newsitem.title: GERMANY: Struggle over control of Eramet goes on.
newsitem.headline: Struggle over control of Eramet goes on.

text.p: Mining group Eramet said it was unlikely a row with the French government over company strategy and mining assets would be settled before general elections at the end of May or even by the end of June.
Eramet executives were talking to journalists in Germany ahead of a nickel and stainless steel industry meeting on Wednesday.
Earlier on Tuesday, the group moved to postpone an annual general meeting called for May 29 in order to win time.
"It was a good solution to postpone the meeting," said chairman Yves Rambaud.
"It will give us time to find the best solutions and to find a new composition of the baord to implement policies in favour of all the shareholders."

Staff representatives wanted employees to be given the chance to select three directors from their own ranks because they felt the need to counter government attempts to dominate policy, the Eramet officials said.
Rambaud said the company had set clear commercial objectives and they would remain the same, regardless of the row, whatever composition the future 15-member board might take.
Erap, the state holding with a majority 55-percent stake in the company, on May 7 announced its intentions to appoint three new members to the board of directors and replace Rambaud.
Rambaud said Eramet was in the process of resolving a politically sensitive nickel mine conflict in New Caledonia which was at the heart of the conflict.

Erap wants to encourage a nickel mining licence for Eramet's Koniambo field to be handed over to a new nickel smelter project in the north of the country while Eramet would obtain the right to the Poum field, which is currently in the hands of the local Kanak company SMSP.
SMSP wants to build the new smelter in cooperation with Eramet competitor Falconbridge.
Rambaud said Eramet needed compensation for the loss of Koniambo, which was the larger field, and it needed guarantees to get it back if the smelter project fell through.
"We won't acept the ore body to be withdrawn against our plans and against the island's interest and find the ore is exported to the benefit of Japanese and United States smelters," he said.
These considerations in his view overruled respect for French government intentions to develop the north of the island in order to appease local Kanak separatists.
Eramet officials said it was unclear whether such a move was even necessary to serve the government's obvious wish to win a 1998 referendum on possible independence for the island.
Rambaud said Eramet's nickel production in New Caledonia was mostly in line with schedules although the row had caused some disruption to plant operations and nickel transport.
The third largest nickel producer in the world, Eramet plans to produce 55,000 tonnes of nickel in 1997 after 53,413 tonnes last year.

German board member Wilhelm Scheider said he and the other members representing minority shareholders interests would consider resigning in a move following Swedish board member Stig Ramel if state interference was to grow beyond reason.
The row has put question marks on future French privatisations.
